summary: Describes the tag URI scheme. Tag URIs are designed to be unique across space and time while remaining easy for humans to read and write. They have no authoritative resolution mechanism, and can be used simply as entity identifiers. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A tag is a name that is unique because it includes who made it and when, like labeling a lunchbox with your name and the date. Nobody has to look it up; it just stays distinct.

questions: how to create unique identifiers with tag uri
how to mint a tag uri
subtitle: Identifiers made unique by combining a domain or email address with a date, with no registry needed.

tldr.problem: People need identifiers that are unique across space and time, easy for humans to read and mint, and free of any central registration or built-in lookup mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: A tag URI has the form tag:authority,date:specific. The authority is a domain name or email address, and the date is one on which that entity held it, so the pair identifies one tagging entity.
tldr.outcome: Tags have no authoritative resolution mechanism and are only identifiers. The scheme is registered with IANA as permanent.

today: RFC 4151 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. The tag scheme is registered with IANA as permanent.

sections.title: What Tags Are For
sections.content:
A tag is a URI meant to meet four requirements: identifiers that are likely unique across space and time from a practically inexhaustible supply, convenient for humans to mint and read, needing no central registration (at least for holders of domain names or email addresses), and independent of any resolution scheme.

Other identifiers fall short. UUIDs are hard for humans to read. OIDs and Digital Object Identifiers require registering as a naming authority. Using http URLs as identifiers invites attempts to resolve them, and a new owner of a domain name cannot tell what the previous owner already minted. The RFC also notes that many people hold an email address but not a domain name.
sections.eli5: Other kinds of ID are either unreadable, need you to sign up somewhere, or look like web links that lead nowhere. Tags are meant to be readable and need no sign-up.

sections.title: Tag Syntax
sections.content:
The ABNF is tagURI = "tag:" taggingEntity ":" specific [ "#" fragment ]. The taggingEntity is an authorityName, a comma, and a date. The authority name is a DNS name or an email address, and the domain name MUST be fully qualified. Lowercase is RECOMMENDED.

The specific part is chosen by whoever mints the tag and should be human-friendly. Tags SHOULD NOT be minted with percent-encoded parts. Software MUST NOT reject tags that fall outside this syntax, to leave room for future authority name types.

Examples from the RFC include tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-555 and tag:yaml.org,2002:int.
sections.eli5: A tag reads like a label: the word tag, then who owns it and the day, then the name you picked for the thing.

sections.title: Rules for Minting Tags
sections.content:
The date makes the tagging entity globally unique, because a domain name or email address is assigned to at most one entity at a time. The date is a day, taken in UTC at 00:00, on which the entity held the authority name. It is written as YYYY, YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD, and month and day default to 01.

An entity MUST NOT mint tags under an authority name held by someone else at that moment, and MUST NOT use a future date. Different spellings of the same date, such as 2000 and 2000-01-01, count as distinct tags.

Claiming dates from a period when a name was unassigned MUST NOT be done without substantial evidence. The RFC says the only mechanism the authors know of is daily polling of the whois registry. The tagging entity SHOULD keep records to make its specific identifiers unique, and may delegate parts of its namespace.
sections.eli5: You may only use a name on a day when it was really yours, and never a day in the future. Then the same label cannot be made by two people.

sections.title: Resolution and Equality
sections.content:
There is no authoritative resolution mechanism for tags. They can only be used as identifiers. If authoritative resolution is wanted, a different URI scheme should be used.

Tags are equal only if they are completely indistinguishable in their machine representation with the same character encoding. They are compared character code by character code, so for example tag:EXAMPLE.com,2000: never equals tag:example.com,2000:.
sections.eli5: A tag is just a name, not a web address you can click. Two tags are the same only if every letter matches exactly.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registration
sections.content:
Minting a tag is internal to the tagging entity. The main risks are minting errors, such as misapplying the date rules or sharing an organisational authority name without agreement. A malicious party could also make it appear that a name was assigned to several entities, so tagging entities SHOULD use reputable assigning authorities and verify assignment where possible.

To avoid clock-skew tricks, entities SHOULD use authority names assigned continuously from well before to well after 00:00 UTC on the chosen date. IANA registered the tag scheme with status permanent, and the template names RDF, YAML and Atom as example users.
sections.eli5: The main danger is someone claiming a name they did not really own on that day. So pick names you clearly held for a long time around that date.

data.title: Tag URI syntax
data.code:
tagURI = "tag:" taggingEntity ":" specific [ "#" fragment ]
taggingEntity = authorityName "," date
authorityName = DNSname / emailAddress
date = year ["-" month ["-" day]]
